Scheduled Task Builder

Twelve gates applied before any scheduled task is created or changed, because an ungated task fails silently and its output looks correct.
SKILL · RUNS AUTOMATICALLY WHEN IT APPLIES

What it does

Creates, audits, and repairs Cowork scheduled tasks so they survive unattended deferred runs. A scheduled-task prompt is not a chat prompt. Get a chat prompt wrong and the next message corrects it. Get a scheduled prompt wrong and it runs unattended, at a time nobody chose, in a session with a different mount topology and no conversation history - and the output usually looks fine.

That last part is the whole problem. A fabricated report, a duplicate Slack post, a trend chart built from a history store that was never found, and a genuinely clean run are visually identical. Nobody goes looking for a failure that reports success. This skill exists because 24 live tasks were audited in one sweep and every single one carried at least one defect.

Three modes

ModeUse when
CreateBuilding a new recurring or one-time task
AuditReviewing existing tasks for defects, no changes yet
RepairFixing a task after an audit or a reported misbehavior

The twelve gates

Every produced prompt satisfies each gate or marks it exempt with the reason written into the prompt itself. That second half matters: an exemption with no stated reason looks identical to an oversight, and the next audit will "fix" it. Each gate is here because a real task failed on it in a way that stayed invisible until someone went looking.

  1. Derive the date first, with the timezone pinned explicitly. Deferred runs fire on later days than scheduled, so any day-gated branch silently takes the wrong path - and the inherited timezone is not guaranteed. Day-count thresholds are the sharpest version: a 60-day staleness rule and a 59-day one give opposite verdicts, and nothing in the output reveals which was used.
  2. Dedupe on the current period's output existing, never on the calendar. "If today is the 1st" fails the moment a run defers to the 2nd. "If this month's report already exists" holds. Gate on the artifact.
  3. Mount check that test-reads a known file by absolute path and STOPS. Covering every surface the task reads and writes, placed before the work. A check at write time means an hour of reading with nowhere to put it.
  4. Absolute save paths. One convention, written literally - dedupe gates glob these paths, and a changed shape breaks them silently.
  5. Grep every path and named source against disk before calling a prompt clean. Prompts rot. This gate caught defects in a third of the tasks audited: a task pointing at a deleted folder builds its output from nothing and reports normally.
  6. Mass-change STOP. Any bulk delete, edit, or overwrite gets a volume threshold that halts and asks. A failed API pull looks exactly like "everything was removed."
  7. State advances only on success. Advance a cursor on a failed run and the task silently skips an entire period, forever - the next run never looks back.
  8. Verify the browser's signed-in account. Never gate on a deviceId or a label. Chrome profile labels cannot be renamed and are frequently crossed, so "the logged-in browser" is not an instruction - and the wrong profile does not error, it returns empty, which reads as "no activity this week." But an ID allowlist is not the fix: it was this gate until 2026-08-05, and it failed on its own terms. Extension deviceIds rotate on re-pair or reinstall, so an ID is an identity proxy, not an identity check - when it rotates the gate stops permitting anything and the run reports "not reachable," which looks correct in the log. Two standup tasks lost a source for five consecutive runs that way. Gate on the property, not the handle: read the signed-in account directly and compare it. Right account, proceed; wrong account, report which account was seen and continue without that source. Record an observed deviceId in the run log as an observation, never as an allowlist entry for the next run.
  9. Duplicate-side-effect gate for anything external. Gate the side effect, not the whole run: a re-run should still show its report in chat while skipping the duplicate Slack post.
  10. Single-channel rule. A file bash executes gets mutated via bash; a file the Edit tool touches gets verified via the Read tool. Crossing that boundary makes bash report a phantom syntax error on a perfectly good file.
  11. A partial run must never read as clean. "All green" requires that every check actually ran. An absence of access is not an absence of problems.
  12. Report the literal condition, never a plausible cause. Quote the tool's actual error string. This is the gate that protects all the others - an invented explanation stops the next reader from looking.

Do not cargo-cult the list. Some gates genuinely do not apply - an idempotent task is better off without a dedupe gate, a one-time task has no period to dedupe against, a read-only task needs no save path. When a gate does not apply, the reason is written inside the prompt so the exemption survives the next audit.

Backing up the task

The live task store is the only copy and it is untracked in git, so every create and every repair writes the full prompt body to the backups tree, split by machine (desktop / laptop) because the two machines run different task sets. The schedule metadata - cron, fireAt, enabled, jitter - is refreshed alongside it, since a prompt body alone cannot rebuild a task. This is part of the workflow rather than a periodic chore: a backup that depends on someone remembering is not a backup.

Two operational facts worth knowing

  • A missed run fires on next launch - that deferral is exactly what gates 1 and 2 exist for.
  • Clicking "Run now" once pre-approves the task's tools, so future unattended runs do not stall on a permission prompt. Worth doing immediately for anything touching connectors or the browser, because a run paused on a permission dialog at 3 AM is indistinguishable from a run that never fired.

Hardening is not a bug report

When strengthening a prompt, the skill writes "changed for robustness, both forms verified." It claims a defect only when the target task's own artifacts prove one. A fabricated defect history in a production prompt is worse than the defect would have been, because the next reader believes it and stops looking for the real cause. Repairs also replace the prompt wholesale - there is no patch mode - so the live prompt is read in full and reproduced with the changes folded in, compressing nothing. Those prompts encode corrections someone paid for in a real failure, and a summarized rule is a deleted rule.

Requirements

What this skill needs in order to run. Added 2026-08-20.

Skills - None.

Connectors / MCP servers - scheduled-tasks - required; the skill calls create_scheduled_task / update_scheduled_task.

Folder access - Write access to Backups/scheduled-tasks/[machine]/, where the full prompt body is saved after a task is created or updated.

KB modules / context files - references/gate-failures.md - bundled; the worked failure behind each gate.

Repos - None.

If something is missing - A failed tool call is LOUD. Everything else this skill exists for is SILENT: an ungated task prompt fails and its output still looks correct - a fabricated report, a duplicate post, or a chart built from a history store that was never found are visually identical to a clean run. Twelve gates are applied, or exempted with the reason written into the prompt itself, because an unexplained exemption is indistinguishable from an oversight.
